notes:
1. Health — Meaning and Development Importance

  • Health is broader than the absence of disease.
  • It includes physical, mental and social well-being.
  • Good health improves people's ability to study, work, earn income and participate in society.
  • Poor health can simultaneously reduce household income and increase medical expenditure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Health → Human Capital → Productivity → Economic Development

2. Health — Economic and Social Benefits

A healthier population can contribute to:

  • Higher labour productivity.
  • Better educational outcomes.
  • Lower absenteeism.
  • Greater life expectancy.
  • Better maternal and child development.
  • Lower household vulnerability.
  • Stronger human capital.

3. Public Health — Meaning

  • Public health focuses on protecting and improving the health of populations rather than treating only individual patients.

Important public-health activities include:

  • Disease prevention.
  • Vaccination.
  • Surveillance.
  • Sanitation.
  • Safe drinking water.
  • Maternal and child health.
  • Nutrition.
  • Health education.
  • Epidemic control.
  • Disease screening.

4. Preventive Health Care

  • Preventive care seeks to stop disease before it develops or detect it early.

Examples include:

  • Vaccination.
  • Screening.
  • Nutrition programmes.
  • Tobacco-control measures.
📌 Must-Memorise

Preventive Care → Prevent or Detect Early

5. Promotive Health Care

  • Promotive care encourages healthy behaviour and healthier living conditions.

Examples include:

  • Physical activity.
  • Healthy diet.
  • Sanitation.
  • Health education.

6. Curative, Rehabilitative and Palliative Care

  • Curative care → Diagnoses and treats disease after it develops.
  • Rehabilitative care → Helps restore function after illness, injury or disability.
  • Palliative care → Reduces pain and improves quality of life in serious or life-limiting illness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Preventive → Stop

Promotive → Improve

Curative → Treat

Rehabilitative → Restore

Palliative → Relieve

7. Comprehensive Health Care

Modern comprehensive health care combines:

  • Preventive.
  • Promotive.
  • Curative.
  • Rehabilitative.
  • Palliative services.

8. Universal Health Coverage — UHC

  • UHC stands for Universal Health Coverage.
  • It broadly means people should obtain needed health services without suffering financial hardship.
📌 Must-Memorise

UHC → Needed Health Services + Financial Protection

9. Constitutional Health Framework

  • Article 47 directs the State to regard improvement of public health and raising nutrition and the standard of living as among its primary duties.
  • Public health and sanitation fall primarily within the State List.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 47 → Nutrition + Standard of Living + Public Health

10. Health — Federal Responsibility

State Governments have major responsibility for:

  • Public hospitals.
  • Primary health care.
  • Disease control.
  • Sanitation.
  • Health-service delivery.

The Union Government contributes through:

  • National policy.
  • Centrally supported programmes.
  • Regulation.
  • Research.
  • Disease-control initiatives.
  • Health financing.
  • Inter-State coordination.

11. Article 21 and Health

  • Article 21 protects the right to life.
  • Judicial interpretation has connected protection of life with health and access to health care.
  • For exams, this should be distinguished from Article 47, which expressly mentions public health.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 21 → Judicially Linked to Health

Article 47 → Explicit Directive on Public Health

12. Primary Health Care

  • Primary health care is generally the first level of contact with the formal health system.
  • It focuses on prevention, early detection, common illnesses, maternal and child care, basic treatment and referral.

Facilities can include:

  • Sub Health Centres.
  • Primary Health Centres.
  • Urban Primary Health Centres.
  • Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

13. Secondary Health Care

Secondary care provides:

  • Specialist consultation.
  • Inpatient care.
  • Emergency care.
  • Surgery.
  • Diagnostic services.

Facilities may include:

  • Community Health Centres.
  • Sub-district hospitals.
  • District hospitals.

14. Tertiary Health Care

  • Tertiary care provides highly specialised treatment.

Examples include:

  • Medical college hospitals.
  • Speciality hospitals.
  • Super-speciality institutions.

Services can include:

  • Advanced cardiac care.
  • Cancer treatment.
  • Neurosurgery.
  • Organ transplantation.

15. Referral Pyramid

The preferred referral chain is:

Primary Care

→ Secondary Care

→ Tertiary Care

📌 Must-Memorise

Primary → First Contact

Secondary → Specialist Care

Tertiary → Highly Specialised Care

16. Why Strong Primary Care Matters

  • Strong primary care can prevent minor conditions from becoming severe.
  • It reduces unnecessary pressure on district and tertiary hospitals.
  • It also improves continuity of care.

17. National Health Policy — 2017

  • India's broad national health-policy framework in the supplied source is the National Health Policy, 2017.
  • It was approved by the Union Cabinet on 15 March 2017.
  • It followed the earlier National Health Policy of 2002.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Health Policy → 2017

18. NHP 2017 — Core Priorities

Important priorities include:

  • Universal access.
  • Stronger primary care.
  • Prevention.
  • Quality.
  • Financial protection.
  • Human resources.
  • Regulation.
  • Health-system strengthening.

19. National Health Mission — NHM

  • NHM stands for National Health Mission.
  • It is a major health-system-strengthening programme.

Its two major sub-missions are:

  • National Rural Health Mission.
  • National Urban Health Mission.
📌 Must-Memorise

NHM = NRHM + NUHM

20. National Rural Health Mission — NRHM

  • NRHM was launched on 12 April 2005.
  • It seeks to improve accessible, affordable and quality rural health care.
📌 Must-Memorise

NRHM → 2005

21. National Urban Health Mission — NUHM

  • NUHM was approved in 2013.
  • It focuses especially on health needs of the urban poor and vulnerable populations.
📌 Must-Memorise

NUHM → 2013

22. NHM — Main Programme Areas

NHM includes:

  • Health-system strengthening.
  • Reproductive and maternal health.
  • Newborn, child and adolescent health.
  • Communicable-disease programmes.
  • Non-communicable-disease programmes.
  • Infrastructure support.

23. NHP 2017 vs NHM

  • NHP 2017 → Broad policy direction.
  • NHM → Health-system delivery and strengthening programme.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

National Health Policy ≠ National Health Mission

24. Rural Health — Main Challenges

Rural areas may face:

  • Long distance to hospitals.
  • Specialist shortages.
  • Maternal-health gaps.
  • Communicable diseases.
  • Chronic diseases.
  • Emergency-referral problems.
  • Health-worker shortages.

25. Urban Health — Main Challenges

Urban vulnerable populations may face:

  • Overcrowding.
  • Poor sanitation.
  • Pollution.
  • Occupational risks.
  • Inability to afford care.
  • Unequal access despite nearby hospitals.

26. Continuum of Care

An effective system links:

Community

→ Primary Care

→ Referral Care

→ Follow-Up

📌 Must-Memorise

Health Care Should Continue Beyond Hospital Discharge

27. Ayushman Bharat — Two Major Components

Ayushman Bharat has two complementary pillars:

  • Comprehensive primary health care.
  • Hospitalisation financial protection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ayushman Bharat ≠ PM-JAY Alone

28. Ayushman Arogya Mandir

  • Health and Wellness Centres are now developed under the name Ayushman Arogya Mandir in the supplied source.
  • They provide comprehensive primary health care closer to communities.

29. Ayushman Arogya Mandir — Service Areas

Services can include:

  • Maternal and child health.
  • Communicable diseases.
  • Non-communicable diseases.
  • Oral health.
  • Eye and ENT care.
  • Elderly care.
  • Palliative care.
  • Mental health.
  • First-level emergency care.

30. PM-JAY — Meaning

  • AB PM-JAY stands for Ayushman Bharat–Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana.
  • It provides financial protection for eligible beneficiaries for covered secondary and tertiary hospitalisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

PM-JAY → Hospitalisation Financial Protection

31. PM-JAY — Standard Cover in Source

According to the supplied source:

  • Standard coverage is ₹5 lakh per eligible family per year.
  • Covered treatment is provided through empanelled public and private hospitals.
  • Treatment is designed to be cashless for covered services.
📌 Must-Memorise

PM-JAY → ₹5 Lakh / Eligible Family / Year

32. PM-JAY — Senior Citizens 70+

According to the supplied source:

  • A 2024 expansion brought all senior citizens aged 70 years and above within the applicable AB PM-JAY framework irrespective of socio-economic status.
  • Eligible senior citizens can receive coverage under the applicable scheme rules.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

This is a Current Scheme Fact, Not a Permanent Constitutional Rule

33. Ayushman Arogya Mandir vs PM-JAY

  • Ayushman Arogya Mandir → Primary health care.
  • PM-JAY → Financial protection for covered secondary and tertiary hospitalisation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Primary Care ≠ Hospital Insurance

34. Maternal Health

Important maternal-health services include:

  • Antenatal care.
  • Institutional delivery.
  • Skilled birth attendance.
  • Emergency obstetric care.
  • Postnatal care.

35. RMNCH+A Continuum

The continuum can be understood as:

Reproductive Health

→ Pregnancy

→ Birth

→ Newborn

→ Child

→ Adolescent

36. Infant Mortality Rate — IMR

  • IMR stands for Infant Mortality Rate.
  • It measures deaths of infants below one year per 1,000 live births.
📌 Must-Memorise

IMR → Infant Deaths / 1,000 Live Births

37. Maternal Mortality Ratio — MMR

  • MMR stands for Maternal Mortality Ratio.
  • It is conventionally expressed as maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
📌 Must-Memorise

MMR → Maternal Deaths / 100,000 Live Births

38. IMR vs MMR

  • IMR → Infant deaths.
  • MMR → Maternal deaths.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

IMR → per 1,000

MMR → per 100,000

39. Child and Adolescent Health

Child-health interventions include:

  • Newborn care.
  • Immunisation.
  • Nutrition.
  • Childhood-disease management.
  • Early diagnosis.

Adolescent health includes:

  • Nutrition.
  • Reproductive health.
  • Mental health.
  • Substance-abuse prevention.
  • Injury prevention.

40. Immunisation

  • Immunisation protects individuals and communities from vaccine-preventable diseases.
  • Vaccination stimulates the immune system to develop protection against specific infections.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vaccination → Preventive Health Intervention

41. Universal Immunisation Programme

  • India operates a national immunisation programme using the National Immunisation Schedule.
  • Immunisation helps reduce child mortality, outbreaks and disability.

42. Herd Protection

  • When a sufficiently large share of a population is immune to a particular infectious disease, transmission can become more difficult.
  • The required level differs by disease and vaccine.

43. Preventive Screening

Important screening areas include:

  • Hypertension.
  • Diabetes.
  • Certain cancers.
  • Early detection can reduce complications and treatment costs.

44. Communicable Diseases — Meaning

  • Communicable diseases can spread directly or indirectly through persons, vectors, food, water or the environment.

Examples include:

  • Tuberculosis.
  • Malaria.
  • Dengue.
  • HIV infection.
  • Leprosy.
  • Viral hepatitis.

45. Communicable-Disease Control

Major measures include:

  • Surveillance.
  • Early diagnosis.
  • Treatment.
  • Vaccination where available.
  • Vector control.
  • Safe water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Health education.

46. Tuberculosis — TB

  • Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • It commonly affects the lungs but can affect other organs.
  • Control requires diagnosis, complete treatment, follow-up and prevention of drug resistance.
📌 Must-Memorise

TB → Mycobacterium tuberculosis

47. Vector-Borne Diseases

Examples include:

  • Malaria.
  • Dengue.
  • Chikungunya.
  • Lymphatic filariasis.

Control can involve:

  • Eliminating mosquito breeding sites.
  • Environmental sanitation.
  • Personal protection.
  • Surveillance.

48. Antimicrobial Resistance — AMR

  • Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms become less responsive to medicines used to treat infection.
  • Responsible antibiotic use and surveillance are important.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Antibiotics Should Not Automatically Be Used for Viral Infections

49. Non-Communicable Diseases — NCDs

  • NCD stands for Non-Communicable Disease.
  • They generally do not spread directly from person to person.

Major examples include:

  • Cardiovascular disease.
  • Diabetes.
  • Cancer.
  • Chronic respiratory disease.

50. Major NCD Risk Factors

Important modifiable risk factors include:

  • Tobacco use.
  • Harmful alcohol use.
  • Physical inactivity.
  • Unhealthy diet.
  • Obesity.

51. Hypertension

  • Hypertension means persistently elevated blood pressure.
  • It is a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke and kidney disease.

52. Diabetes

  • Diabetes involves abnormal regulation of blood glucose.
  • Complications can affect:
  • Heart.
  • Kidneys.
  • Eyes.
  • Nerves.
  • Blood vessels.

53. NCD Management Chain

Prevention

→ Screening

→ Early Treatment

→ Long-Term Follow-Up

📌 Must-Memorise

NCD Care Requires Continuity, Not One-Time Treatment

54. Double Burden of Disease

  • India simultaneously faces communicable diseases and non-communicable diseases.
📌 Must-Memorise

Double Burden of Disease → Communicable + NCDs

55. Social Determinants of Health

Health is influenced by factors outside hospitals, including:

  • Nutrition.
  • Income.
  • Education.
  • Housing.
  • Drinking water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Employment.
  • Environment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Health Begins Outside Hospitals Too

56. Double Burden of Malnutrition

  • Undernutrition can coexist with overweight and obesity.
  • This is referred to as a double burden of malnutrition.

57. Water, Sanitation and Health

  • Safe drinking water and sanitation reduce exposure to many infectious diseases.
  • Public health therefore requires coordination across health, nutrition, water, sanitation, housing and education.

58. Health Financing — Meaning

Health care is financed through combinations of:

  • Public expenditure.
  • Insurance or assurance.
  • Household expenditure.
  • Other financing sources.

59. Out-of-Pocket Expenditure — OOPE

  • OOPE stands for Out-of-Pocket Expenditure.
  • It refers to direct health expenditure paid by households from their own resources.
📌 Must-Memorise

OOPE → Direct Household Health Spending

60. Why High OOPE Is a Problem

A serious illness may force households to:

  • Use savings.
  • Borrow.
  • Sell assets.
  • Reduce spending on food or education.
  • Financial protection is therefore a central health-policy objective.

61. Public Health Services vs Financial Protection

Public health services provide:

  • Hospitals.
  • Primary care.
  • Medicines.
  • Diagnostics.
  • Health workers.
  • Vaccination.
  • Surveillance.

Financial protection:

  • Reduces the burden of large treatment costs.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Insurance Alone ≠ Universal Health Coverage

62. Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission — ABDM

  • ABDM stands for Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.
  • It seeks to create digital infrastructure for an integrated health ecosystem.
📌 Must-Memorise

ABDM → Digital Health Infrastructure

63. ABHA

  • ABHA stands for Ayushman Bharat Health Account.
  • It provides a digital health identifier within the applicable system.
  • It supports consent-based exchange of health information.
📌 Must-Memorise

ABHA → Digital Health Identifier

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

ABHA ≠ Health Insurance Policy

64. Digital Health Registries

ABDM supports digital registries for:

  • Health facilities.
  • Health professionals.

65. Telemedicine

  • Telemedicine uses telecommunications technology to provide medical consultation or support when the patient and provider are in different locations.

It can help with:

  • Remote areas.
  • Specialist consultations.
  • Follow-up care.
  • Screening.
  • Referral.

66. Digital Health — Benefits and Risks

Benefits include:

  • Continuity of care.
  • Better records.
  • Referral support.
  • Data-based planning.
  • Consultation access.

Challenges include:

  • Privacy.
  • Data security.
  • Consent.
  • Digital literacy.
  • Connectivity.

67. Health Workforce

Important health workers include:

  • Doctors.
  • Nurses.
  • Pharmacists.
  • Laboratory technicians.
  • Public-health specialists.
  • Community health workers.
  • Allied health professionals.

68. ASHA

  • ASHA stands for Accredited Social Health Activist.
  • ASHAs are community-level health workers under NHM.

Functions include:

  • Health awareness.
  • Maternal and child-health support.
  • Immunisation mobilisation.
  • Community follow-up.
  • Referral support.
📌 Must-Memorise

ASHA → Community Link Worker

69. ANM

  • ANM stands for Auxiliary Nurse Midwife.
  • ANMs perform important maternal, child-health, immunisation and community-health functions.
📌 Must-Memorise

ANM → Auxiliary Nurse Midwife

70. Community Health Officer

  • Community Health Officers support comprehensive primary care at upgraded sub-centre-level facilities under the Ayushman Arogya Mandir framework.

71. ASHA vs ANM vs CHO

  • ASHA → Community mobilisation and link role.
  • ANM → Maternal, child and community-health services.
  • CHO → Comprehensive primary-care role at upgraded facilities.

72. Health-Worker Distribution

  • National availability of health professionals does not guarantee equitable local access.
  • Rural and remote areas may still face severe shortages.
📌 Must-Memorise

Health Workforce Challenge → Number + Distribution

73. Tamil Nadu — Public-Health Approach

  • Tamil Nadu has an extensive public-health and medical-care system involving primary facilities, Government hospitals, medical colleges and specialised institutions.
  • Detailed institutional structure belongs to the later Health System in Tamil Nadu chapter.

74. Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam — MTM

  • Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam was launched on 5 August 2021.
  • It provides home-based and continuing health services, particularly for NCDs and persons requiring ongoing care.
📌 Must-Memorise

MTM → 5 August 2021 → Doorstep Health Care

75. MTM — Major Services

Services can include:

  • Delivery of medicines for hypertension and diabetes to specified beneficiaries.
  • Screening.
  • Follow-up.
  • Palliative care.
  • Physiotherapy.
  • Referral.
📌 Must-Memorise

MTM → Hospital-Centred Care to Doorstep Care

76. Chief Minister's Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme — CMCHIS

  • CMCHIS is a Tamil Nadu health-financing programme intended to improve access to hospital treatment for eligible families.
  • The supplied source notes current convergence with AB PM-JAY arrangements.
📌 Must-Memorise

CMCHIS → Hospital-Treatment Financial Protection

77. CMCHIS — Current Source-Dated Eligibility Fact

According to the supplied source:

  • The current annual family-income eligibility limit is below ₹1.20 lakh, subject to scheme conditions.
  • This should be treated as a current scheme fact rather than a permanent constitutional fact.

78. Innuyir Kappom – Nammai Kaakkum 48

  • This Tamil Nadu initiative focuses on life-saving treatment during the critical first 48 hours after road-traffic accidents.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nammai Kaakkum 48 → Road Accident Emergency Care

79. Golden Hours in Trauma Care

  • Rapid emergency treatment immediately after serious trauma can significantly affect survival and disability outcomes.
  • Nammai Kaakkum 48 reflects this principle.

80. Padham Padhukappom

  • Padham Padhukappom is associated in the supplied source with screening and prevention of diabetic-foot complications.
📌 Must-Memorise

Padham Padhukappom → Diabetic-Foot Care

81. Tamil Nadu Health Initiative Mapping

  • Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam → Doorstep NCD and continuing care.
  • CMCHIS → Hospital-treatment financial protection.
  • Nammai Kaakkum 48 → Road-accident trauma care.
  • Padham Padhukappom → Diabetic-foot screening and prevention.

82. Major Health-System Challenges

Important challenges include:

  • Unequal access.
  • Rural specialist shortages.
  • High OOPE.
  • Health-worker shortages.
  • Communicable diseases.
  • NCDs.
  • Population ageing.
  • Mental-health needs.
  • Antimicrobial resistance.
  • Climate-related health risks.
  • Digital divide.
  • Quality of care.

83. Population Ageing — Health Impact

Ageing increases demand for:

  • Geriatric care.
  • Chronic-disease management.
  • Rehabilitation.
  • Palliative care.
  • Long-term care.
  • Social support.
  • This is especially relevant for Tamil Nadu because demographic ageing is progressing comparatively rapidly in the supplied material.

84. Mental Health

  • Mental health is an important component of overall health.
  • Health systems need:
  • Counselling.
  • Psychiatric services.
  • Community support.
  • Stigma reduction.

85. Climate Change and Health

Climate change can increase:

  • Heat-related illness.
  • Vector-borne disease risk.
  • Water-borne diseases.
  • Food-security risks.
  • Disaster injuries.

86. Quality of Care

Access to a facility alone is not sufficient.

Quality requires:

  • Correct diagnosis.
  • Appropriate treatment.
  • Patient safety.
  • Dignity.
  • Continuity of care.
📌 Must-Memorise

Access ≠ Quality

87. Future Health-System Priority

A strong health system requires:

Prevention

  • Primary Care
  • Hospitals
  • Financial Protection
  • Technology
  • Human Resources

95. TNPSC Traps

  • Health is broader than absence of disease.
  • Public health and clinical medicine are related but different.
  • Article 47 specifically refers to public health and nutrition.
  • Article 47 is a Directive Principle.
  • Public health and sanitation are primarily State List subjects.
  • Primary, secondary and tertiary care are different.
  • Primary Health Centre is not a tertiary-care institution.
  • Prevention and treatment are not the same.
  • NHP 2017 and NHM are different.
  • NHP 2017 → Policy framework.
  • NHM → Health-system programme.
  • NRHM → 2005.
  • NUHM → 2013.
  • Ayushman Bharat is broader than PM-JAY.
  • Ayushman Arogya Mandir → Primary care.
  • PM-JAY → Hospitalisation financial protection.
  • PM-JAY does not replace primary health care.
  • PM-JAY standard cover in source → ₹5 lakh per eligible family per year.
  • 70+ senior-citizen expansion is a current scheme fact.
  • IMR and MMR are different.
  • IMR → per 1,000 live births.
  • MMR → per 100,000 live births.
  • Communicable and non-communicable diseases are different.
  • Antibiotics should not automatically be used for viral illness.
  • OOPE means direct household health expenditure.
  • High OOPE can create financial hardship.
  • Health insurance alone cannot create UHC.
  • ABDM is digital health infrastructure.
  • ABHA is a digital health identifier, not insurance.
  • ASHA and ANM are different roles.
  • Health-worker availability and distribution are both important.
  • Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam and CMCHIS are different.
  • MTM → Doorstep continuing care.
  • CMCHIS → Hospital financial protection.
  • Nammai Kaakkum 48 → Emergency road-accident care.
  • Padham Padhukappom → Diabetic-foot care.
  • Detailed Tamil Nadu health-system structure belongs to Chapter 38.

  • Vector-borne disease examples? → Malaria, dengue, chikungunya and filariasis.
  • AMR means? → Antimicrobial resistance.
  • NCD full form? → Non-Communicable Disease.
  • Major NCDs? → Cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, cancer and chronic respiratory diseases.
  • Major NCD risk factors? → Tobacco, alcohol, inactivity, unhealthy diet and obesity.
  • Double burden of disease? → Communicable diseases + NCDs.
  • Social determinants of health? → Income, education, housing, nutrition, water, sanitation, employment and environment.
  • OOPE full form? → Out-of-Pocket Expenditure.
  • Why is high OOPE harmful? → Can force borrowing, asset sales and reduced essential spending.
  • ABDM full form? → Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.
  • ABHA full form? → Ayushman Bharat Health Account.
  • ABHA is insurance? → No.
  • ASHA full form? → Accredited Social Health Activist.
  • ANM full form? → Auxiliary Nurse Midwife.
  • Health-worker challenge? → Number + Distribution.
  • Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam launched? → 5 August 2021.
  • MTM focus? → Doorstep NCD and continuing care.
  • CMCHIS focus? → Hospital-treatment financial protection.
  • Nammai Kaakkum 48 focus? → Emergency trauma treatment after road accidents.
  • Padham Padhukappom associated with? → Diabetic-foot screening and care.
  • Core health-system chain? → Prevention → Primary Care → Referral Hospitals → Financial Protection → Follow-Up.
  • Core institutional chain? → NHP 2017 → NHM → Ayushman Arogya Mandirs → PM-JAY → ABDM.
  • Core Tamil Nadu chain? → MTM → CMCHIS → Nammai Kaakkum 48 → Padham Padhukappom.
